verses.text: For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles,
If ye have heard of the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me to you-ward:
How that by revelation he made known unto me the mystery; (as I wrote afore in few words,
Whereby, when ye read, ye may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ)
Which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men, as it is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit;
That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel:
Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power.
Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given, that I should preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ;
And to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God, who created all things by Jesus Christ:
To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God,
According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord:
In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him.
Wherefore I desire that ye faint not at my tribulations for you, which is your glory.
For this cause I bow my knees unto the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,
Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named,
That he would grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man;
That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith; that ye, being rooted and grounded in love,
May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height;
And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge, that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God.
Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us,
Unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen.

summary: Paul begins a prayer and does not finish it for thirteen verses. "For this cause I Paul, the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles" breaks off mid-thought, and the sentence is only resumed at verse fourteen with the same words, "For this cause I bow my knees." What interrupts is a digression about his own commission, and the interruption turns out to be necessary, because the readers cannot pray the prayer until they know why the man praying it is in chains. He describes his office as an administration entrusted rather than a career achieved — "the dispensation of the grace of God which is given me to you-ward" — and its content as something he did not work out but received: "by revelation he made known unto me the mystery." The word mystery here means a secret now disclosed rather than a truth permanently obscure, and Paul is careful to say both that it "in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men" and that it "is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit," so the disclosure is neither private to him nor a novelty of his own devising. Then he states the secret in one line, and it is not what a religious imagination would predict: "That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel." The hidden purpose of the ages is a merger. Paul's own place in it is described with a superlative that outdoes ordinary modesty — "Unto me, who am less than the least of all saints, is this grace given" — and the commission has two parts, to "preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ" and "to make all men see what is the fellowship of the mystery, which from the beginning of the world hath been hid in God." Verse ten then makes the most startling claim in the letter: the audience for this disclosure is not only human. "To the intent that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God" — the united Church is itself the exhibition, and the watching intelligences are the ones being instructed. This is said to be "According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord," and its practical fruit for the reader is immediate access: "In whom we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him." Only then does Paul return to his chains, and he does so to protect his readers rather than himself: "Wherefore I desire that ye faint not at my tribulations for you, which is your glory." The prayer resumes on his knees, addressed to "the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, Of whom the whole family in heaven and earth is named," and it asks for a series of things that escalate past what a petition normally dares. First strength — "according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with might by his Spirit in the inner man" — then indwelling, "That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith," then stability in love, "being rooted and grounded in love," the metaphors of a plant and a building set side by side. What all of this is for is comprehension, and the object is given only in dimensions without a noun: "May be able to comprehend with all saints what is the breadth, and length, and depth, and height." Paul then names it and immediately concedes the impossibility: "And to know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge." The final clause asks for more than any of the preceding: "that ye might be filled with all the fulness of God." Aware that he has prayed past the edge of what can be requested, Paul closes not with amen but with a doxology that makes the excess into the point: "Now unto him that is able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think, according to the power that worketh in us, Unto him be glory in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages, world without end. Amen."
takeaways: Paul's self-description controls the whole chapter. He is "the prisoner of Jesus Christ for you Gentiles," which reassigns the credit for his imprisonment away from Rome and toward Christ, and away from his own misfortune toward their benefit. He calls himself "less than the least of all saints" — a deliberately impossible comparative, as though the superlative were not low enough — and describes his commission as grace given rather than authority earned. The effect is that the most consequential ministry in the letter is presented as entirely derivative: a secret he did not deduce, an office he did not seek, a power he does not supply, and a suffering whose value belongs to somebody else.

The content of the mystery is the part most often blurred. Paul does not say the mystery is that God saves sinners, or that Christ died, or that grace is free; he says it is "That the Gentiles should be fellowheirs, and of the same body, and partakers of his promise in Christ by the gospel." Three compound words, each stressing togetherness, define the hidden purpose of the ages as the abolition of a religious frontier. That the epoch-making secret of God turns out to be the seating of former outsiders at the same table sets a permanent standard: any Christianity that quietly reinstates a first and second class of members has not merely failed at manners, it has obscured the specific thing God kept hidden for ages in order to reveal.

Verse ten reverses the expected direction of instruction. The Church is not primarily being taught here; she is the lesson — "that now unto the principalities and powers in heavenly places might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God." The word rendered "manifold" suggests something many-coloured or intricately variegated, and what displays it is the improbable composition of a congregation containing people who had no business being in the same room. Angelic and hostile powers alike learn God's wisdom by observation of a mixed community, which means that reconciled diversity in the Church is not a social bonus attached to the gospel but part of its public demonstration in the unseen world.

The prayer of verses sixteen through nineteen is built as a sequence in which each request is the ground of the next, and the sequence moves from interior to immeasurable. Strength in "the inner man" makes room for Christ to "dwell in your hearts by faith"; indwelling produces rootedness "in love"; rootedness is what makes comprehension possible; comprehension terminates in knowing a love that "passeth knowledge"; and knowing that love ends in being "filled with all the fulness of God." Notably the comprehension is corporate — "with all saints" — so the dimensions cannot be measured alone. Paul assumes that the love of Christ is too large for any single Christian's perception and that the missing dimensions are held by other people.

The four dimensions are given without an object, and the omission is probably deliberate. "The breadth, and length, and depth, and height" names a magnitude in every direction without saying of what, and only the next clause supplies a candidate in "the love of Christ." The construction leaves the reader momentarily measuring nothing at all, which is the correct posture, and it is immediately followed by the admission that the thing measured "passeth knowledge." Paul is not being vague; he is asking for a knowledge that includes the recognition of its own insufficiency, a comprehension that grasps enough to know it has not grasped the whole. Devotion that claims to have taken the measure of Christ's love has misunderstood the prayer.

The doxology answers a problem the prayer itself created. Having asked for fulness with "all the fulness of God," Paul has requested something no petitioner can expect, and rather than retreat he escalates: God is "able to do exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think." The measure of that ability is then located not in heaven but in the reader — "according to the power that worketh in us" — so that the same power that raised and seated Christ is named as already operative in an ordinary congregation. And the glory is directed to a specific address, "in the church by Christ Jesus throughout all ages," pairing the community and her Lord as the joint site where God's praise is rendered in time.

crossRefs.label: Acts 9:15 — he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles
crossRefs.why: The narrative of Paul's calling supplies the event behind his claim that "by revelation he made known unto me the mystery." Luke reports both the unsought nature of the encounter and the specific assignment to the nations, and adds the note that he would be shown "how great things he must suffer for my name," which explains why Paul can present his imprisonment as an ordinary feature of the commission rather than an interruption of it. The story also accounts for the extremity of "less than the least of all saints," since the man sent to the Gentiles had been on the road to arrest believers when he was stopped.

crossRefs.label: Colossians 1:26-27 — the mystery which hath been hid from ages... which is Christ in you, the hope of glory
crossRefs.why: Colossians uses the same vocabulary of a mystery hidden from ages and now made manifest, and states the Gentile dimension explicitly in "the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles." It also parallels the peculiar way Ephesians treats apostolic suffering as beneficial to the readers, since Paul there rejoices in his sufferings "for you" and speaks of filling up what remains of the afflictions of Christ for his body's sake. Reading the two together clarifies that "my tribulations for you, which is your glory" is not rhetorical flourish but a settled conviction about how apostolic hardship functions in the life of the churches.

crossRefs.label: 1 Peter 1:12 — which things the angels desire to look into
crossRefs.why: Peter offers the closest parallel to the strange claim of verse ten that angelic powers are the audience of the gospel's disclosure. There the prophets searched and the angels stoop to look at things now reported to the churches, so the drama of salvation is watched from outside human history. Set beside "might be known by the church the manifold wisdom of God," it establishes that the New Testament writers thought of ordinary congregational life as observed by intelligences who are learning something from it — a perspective that raises the stakes of visible unity considerably above the level of institutional convenience.

crossRefs.label: Hebrews 4:16 — let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace
crossRefs.why: Ephesians states almost without explanation that "we have boldness and access with confidence by the faith of him," and Hebrews supplies the reasoning: a high priest who has passed into the heavens and was tempted as we are makes approach both possible and unafraid. The pairing is useful because Ephesians derives access from the disclosure of the mystery and the reconciliation of the two peoples, while Hebrews derives it from priesthood and sacrifice; together they show that the same confidence is being argued from ecclesial and liturgical directions at once.

crossRefs.label: Romans 11:33 — O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments
crossRefs.why: Romans reaches the identical destination by a different road: a long argument about Jew and Gentile that ends in a doxology about unsearchable riches and wisdom, and even uses the word mystery for the arrangement by which the nations are brought in. The verbal overlap with "the unsearchable riches of Christ" and "the manifold wisdom of God" is close enough to suggest a settled pattern in Paul's thinking, in which reflection on the inclusion of the Gentiles reliably terminates in praise rather than in a system. It also supplies the note Ephesians assumes but does not state, that Israel's place in the arrangement is not abolished.

crossRefs.label: John 14:23 — we will come unto him, and make our abode with him
crossRefs.why: Paul prays "That Christ may dwell in your hearts by faith," and the promise in the upper room supplies the theology behind the request: the Father and the Son come and take up residence with the one who keeps Christ's word, and the Spirit is given as the agent of that presence. The parallel also explains the odd structure of the Ephesian prayer, in which the Spirit strengthens the inner man so that Christ may dwell there, since in John the indwelling is a joint and Trinitarian act rather than a series of separate visits.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 12:3 — in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed
crossRefs.why: The promise to Abraham is the oldest form of the secret Paul says was "hid in God," and its presence in the text raises the question of what exactly was hidden. The nations' blessing was announced from the beginning; what was not disclosed was the manner — that they would be "fellowheirs, and of the same body," incorporated on equal terms rather than admitted as clients. Reading the promise behind the mystery keeps Paul's claim from sounding like a rupture with Israel's scriptures, and shows him arguing that the ancient covenant is being executed rather than replaced.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading fastens on the phrase "is now revealed unto his holy apostles and prophets by the Spirit" as evidence that revelation is given to and through a body of commissioned witnesses rather than to individuals reading in isolation. Paul insists that the mystery came to him by revelation, but he immediately places that revelation alongside what was given to the other apostles, so the criterion of authenticity is agreement with an apostolic company and not private certainty. The tradition draws from this the conviction that the deposit of revelation is entrusted to the Church and handed on within her living teaching, so that Scripture is read inside the community that received it rather than over against her. The chapter's climax reinforces this, since the wisdom of God is made known "by the church" — the community is the organ of the disclosure, not merely its beneficiary.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters emphasise that Paul directs the readers to a written text as the check on his claims — "as I wrote afore in few words, Whereby, when ye read, ye may understand my knowledge in the mystery of Christ" — and take this as evidence that the apostolic message was from the outset committed to writing precisely so that ordinary hearers could verify it for themselves. On this reading the apostles and prophets are foundational and unrepeatable, and the mystery once revealed is now possessed in the apostolic writings rather than in a continuing office of disclosure. Many also note that the Church in verse ten displays God's wisdom to the powers rather than defining it. Both traditions agree that the revelation is not privately generated, that it came through the apostles, and that no later authority may add a new mystery to the one Paul says has been made known.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "my tribulations for you, which is your glory," Catholic interpretation reads apostolic suffering as genuinely fruitful for others rather than merely exemplary. Paul does not say his sufferings encourage them or illustrate a principle; he says the tribulations are for them and are their glory, which the tradition understands in terms of a real solidarity in the body whereby one member's affliction, joined to Christ's own passion, benefits the rest. This underwrites the Church's practice of offering suffering in union with Christ for the good of others and her conviction that the communion of saints involves an actual exchange of spiritual goods across the body. Nothing is added to the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice; what is affirmed is that his members are permitted to participate in its application in ways that genuinely help one another.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters typically read the verse in a more direct sense: Paul's imprisonment is their glory because it is the proof and price of the gospel having reached them, and because a suffering apostle vindicates rather than discredits the message. They resist any construction in which human suffering possesses redemptive value, insisting that Christ's passion is complete and unrepeatable and that believers benefit others by proclamation, service and prayer rather than by a transfer of merit. Many add that Paul's stated concern is pastoral — "that ye faint not" — so the sentence functions to steady readers who might read his chains as failure. Both traditions hold that suffering for the gospel is not wasted, that it belongs to apostolic ministry rather than contradicting it, and that Christ's own sacrifice needs no supplement.

interpretationNotes.claim: The prayer that the readers "might be filled with all the fulness of God" is read in Catholic tradition as language of real participation in the divine life, not merely of moral improvement or of a legal relation. Grace is understood to effect a genuine transformation of the person, so that the God who is comprehended in love actually indwells and communicates his own life, and the saints are made partakers of the divine nature without ceasing to be creatures. This underlies the tradition's confidence that sanctification is a real ontological change progressively worked out, that holiness is genuinely attainable by grace in this life, and that the beatific vision toward which the prayer strains is continuous with what is begun now. Verse twenty then guards the whole against presumption by locating the power in God, who does "exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think."

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters affirm the Spirit's real indwelling and progressive sanctification while ordinarily preferring relational and covenantal language to that of infused participation, and insisting that the believer's standing before God never rests on the degree of transformation achieved. Many read "filled with all the fulness of God" as a corporate prayer for the Church to be filled with God's presence and character, pointing to "with all saints" in the preceding verse, rather than as a description of individual ontological elevation. Some also stress that the prayer is asked, not reported, and remains eschatological in reach. Both traditions agree that the goal of Christian life is God himself rather than a benefit obtained from him, that the change worked in believers is genuine and not fictional, and that the whole is powered by God rather than achieved by effort.

authoring.attributionNotes: Original synthesis grounded in the KJV text and the general Catholic/Christian interpretive tradition. No specific published source is quoted or cited; tradition labels denote a position, not a copied source.
